newsitem.title: UK: Hopes rise of AIDS vaccine after test on monkeys.
newsitem.headline: Hopes rise of AIDS vaccine after test on monkeys.

text.p: A vaccine that protected an entire test group of monkeys against the HIV virus offers the freshest hope for a defence against the AIDS epidemic, scientists said on Monday.
Advances in genetics have helped researchers map out precise routes for attacking scourges like HIV, tuberculosis and hepatitis and open the door to real protection, they told a news conference.
"I think there has been a revolution in the past six months," said Thomas Lehner, an immunologist at Guy's Hospital in London who led the study into the monkey vaccine.
The vaccine was a genetically engineered version of the virus, injected into seven HIV-infected macaques.

The macaques were infected rectally, to simulate the sexual transmission that most commonly spreads AIDS around the world, and then the vaccine was injected in their groins to target lymph glands that cleanse this area of the body.
Lehner said every macaque got some sort of protection against the virus.
Four of the seven macaques showed complete immunity, one had "transient" levels of virus and the other two had levels of the virus in their blood drop by 90 percent.
In contrast, 13 of 14 macaques exposed to HIV but not immunised all had high levels of HIV infection.
"We don't know how long the protection lasts," he admitted. The animals were killed and autopsied after six months.
Lehner, speaking ahead of a presentation at the British Association for the Advancement of Science annual festival, said the vaccine was precisely targeted using molecular genetics.
Scientists can now model the inside and outside of viruses, too tiny to be seen except with an electron microscope. They can plot out exactly how their protein envelopes look.

Lehner's vaccine homed in on gp-120, which he described as a little "knob" on the virus envelope, and p-27, a protein inside the virus. It primed the immune system to recognise and attack anything that contained these two proteins.

Such technology can also work against other diseases. "With molecular genetics we can take a virus apart," said Douglas Young, a professor of immunology at Imperial College School of Medicine in London, who is working on a tuberculosis vaccine.
He estimated that TB now infects a third of the world's population, making a vaccine a top priority. To make matters worse, TB is spreading fastest in AIDS victims.
HIV, hepatitis and tuberculosis all pose similar challenges -- they evade drugs and vaccines because they attack a number of targets in the body in a variety of ways.
Even worse, some microbes mutate, thereby dodging successful vaccines. Antibiotic-resistant tuberculosis is one example.
Kenneth Murray, a virologist at the University of Edinburgh said even though effective vaccines exist against hepatitis A and B new forms of the virus were evolving.
"Mutants of hepatitis B virus have emerged which evade the immunity conferred by vaccination, thus providing a new reservoir of infection," he said.
